name: Clorazepate (Tranxene)
summary: Long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety and focal seizures. High risk of sedation, dependence, and withdrawal; use short term, avoid with opioids, and taper very slowly.
description: Clorazepate is a long-acting benzodiazepine that is FDA-approved for anxiety disorders and as an add-on medication for focal (partial) seizures. In psychiatry, it is considered an older, long-duration benzodiazepine and is generally reserved for short-term relief of severe anxiety when other treatments are ineffective or still taking effect. Because it is converted in the body to nordiazepam, which has a very long half-life, clorazepate can accumulate, leading to prolonged sedation and high fall risk in older adults. Like all benzodiazepines, it carries serious risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, and life-threatening withdrawal if stopped abruptly. Concomitant use with opioids or other sedatives markedly increases the risk of respiratory depression, coma, and death.
patient_summary: Clorazepate (often known by the brand name Tranxene) is a long-acting "benzo" used for anxiety and certain types of seizures. It can be very calming, but it also makes many people drowsy, unsteady, and mentally slower, especially as it builds up in the body. Because it is long-acting, it can stay in your system for days. Like all benzodiazepines, it can be habit-forming, and your body can become physically dependent on it. Stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause severe withdrawal, including seizures, and can be dangerous. The safest use is usually short-term, at the lowest effective dose, while longer-term treatments like therapy or antidepressants are started. It should be used with extreme caution—if at all—together with opioids, alcohol, or other sedating medications.

linked_conditions.context: May be used short term for severe anxiety while SSRIs/SNRIs and therapy are started. Not recommended as long-term monotherapy due to dependence, cognitive effects, and fall risk.
Sometimes used historically for panic, but shorter-acting benzodiazepines are more common. Current guidelines favor SSRIs/SNRIs and CBT; benzodiazepines are reserved for refractory cases.
FDA-approved as adjunctive therapy for focal (partial) seizures. Tolerance to antiseizure effects can develop over time; generally not used as first-line in newer epilepsy regimens.
High risk of misuse and addiction. Use should generally be avoided in patients with active or past substance use disorders unless there is a compelling reason and close monitoring.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to clorazepate or any component of the formulation
Severe respiratory compromise (eg, significant COPD, sleep apnea) where benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression would be dangerous
High-risk concurrent opioid therapy unless alternatives are inadequate and risk mitigation is in place
History of benzodiazepine use disorder, unless used only in tightly controlled, short-term settings

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Effective as an anxiolytic and antiseizure agent, but long half-life and side effect profile limit its use compared to newer options. Tolerance frequently develops to antiseizure effects with chronic use.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Clorazepate can reliably reduce anxiety and help prevent some types of seizures, but its long-lasting sedative effects and high dependence risk mean that many clinicians now reserve it for specific situations and limit how long it is used.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Long-acting benzodiazepine; efficacy must be weighed carefully against safety risks.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapidly decarboxylated in the acidic environment of the stomach to its active metabolite nordiazepam before absorption.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: High oral bioavailability; food has minimal impact on total exposure but may slow absorption slightly.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Sedation and anxiolysis typically begin within 30–60 minutes after an oral dose.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 0.5–2 hours for peak serum levels of active metabolite.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Nordiazepam, the main active metabolite, has a very long half-life (approximately 20–160 hours), leading to accumulation with repeated dosing.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Clinically significant sedation and anxiolysis may extend into the next day, especially with evening dosing or in older adults.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Prodrug; rapidly converted to nordiazepam (active), then hepatically metabolized via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to oxazepam (active) and subsequently glucuronidated.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily excreted in urine as conjugated metabolites (about two-thirds), with some fecal excretion.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken with or without food; taking with food or water can reduce stomach upset.

sections.heading: What It's Used For (Psychiatry-Focused)
sections.text: Clorazepate is a long-acting benzodiazepine, so psychiatry generally treats it as a secondary or last-line option, not a first choice.
items: Short-term relief of severe {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:anxiety disorders}: Used for acute symptom control while first-line treatments (SSRIs/SNRIs, psychotherapy) are initiated.
Adjunctive treatment of focal (partial) seizures: Primarily managed by neurology; important for psychiatrists to know in patients with comorbid epilepsy and anxiety.
Bridge therapy: Temporary use during crisis or severe exacerbation when rapid calming is needed and other options are ineffective or not yet working.

Chronic, low-dose anxiety management (rare): In select, carefully monitored patients who have failed other options, very low doses may be used long term—but risks often outweigh benefits, especially in older adults.
off_label: Other seizure types (eg, myoclonic or atonic seizures) as adjunctive therapy in specialized epilepsy care
Occasional off-label use in refractory anxiety disorders, though this is increasingly discouraged in modern guidelines

sections.heading: What People Often Feel on Clorazepate
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but many people describe a mix of relief and significant sedation or cognitive changes.

quotes: It took the edge off my anxiety within an hour.
I wasn’t constantly on high alert anymore.
I felt a sense of calm that I hadn’t felt in a long time.
I felt very sleepy and slow, especially during the day.
My thinking felt foggy and it was harder to concentrate.
I could function, but it felt like running through mud.
items.note: Because clorazepate is long-acting, drowsiness and cognitive slowing can persist into the next day.

quotes: I felt unsteady when I walked, especially at night.
I stumbled more and needed to be careful on stairs.
My family noticed I moved like I had a few drinks.
items.note: This increased fall risk is a major concern in older adults.

quotes: The same dose didn’t work as well after a while.
If I tried to cut down too quickly, my anxiety exploded.
Missing doses made me feel shaky and awful.
items.note: Physical dependence and withdrawal are common with long-term use and with higher doses.

quotes: Instead of calming me, it made me agitated.
I felt unusually irritable and snappy.
My sleep got more restless, not better.
items.note: Paradoxical agitation, disinhibition, or irritability can occur, especially in younger or older patients or those with certain psychiatric histories.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
sections.text: Clorazepate starts working relatively quickly, but because it turns into a long-acting metabolite, its effects linger for days.
key_points: 30–60 minutes: Typical onset of sedation and anxiety relief after an oral dose.
0.5–2 hours: Time to peak blood levels of the active metabolite (nordiazepam).
All day and often into the next: Sedation, balance issues, and cognitive slowing can persist, especially with repeated dosing.
20–160 hours: Very long half-life of nordiazepam, which means the medication builds up in the body over time.
Several days: Time for blood levels to significantly decrease after stopping—important when planning tapers, surgery, or pregnancy.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.comparison: Effective for anxiety and seizures, but riskier than many newer options.
sections.text: Clorazepate is a potent anxiolytic and can be an effective adjunct for focal seizures. However, its long half-life, high dependence potential, and risk of cognitive and motor impairment have led many clinicians to favor other medications (SSRIs/SNRIs, non-benzodiazepine antiseizure agents, or shorter-acting benzodiazepines in select cases). In modern psychiatric practice, clorazepate is rarely a first-line choice and is usually reserved for special situations where its long duration is specifically desired and risks are carefully managed.
sections.clinical_details: Tolerance develops over time to the antiseizure effects but not fully to the anxiolytic and sedative effects, which can create a difficult balance between seizure control, anxiety relief, and side effects. Long-term use is associated with cognitive impairment, increased fall risk, and complex withdrawal syndromes, especially after high doses or multi-year exposure.

citation.title: Long-acting benzodiazepines in anxiety and epilepsy

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Concomitant use with opioids or other sedatives can cause life-threatening breathing problems. Long-term use can lead to dependence and severe withdrawal.
sections.black_box: Although clorazepate itself does not carry a separate boxed warning beyond the class warnings for benzodiazepines, the key risks are profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death when combined with opioids, and serious abuse, misuse, addiction, and withdrawal risks with ongoing use.
other: Concomitant use with opioids: Combining clorazepate with opioids can lead to deep sedation, dangerously slow or shallow breathing, coma, and death. Use together only when absolutely necessary, at the lowest effective doses, and for the shortest duration possible.
Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Like all benzodiazepines, clorazepate can be misused and is associated with addiction and overdose, particularly when combined with alcohol or other drugs.

Dependence and withdrawal: Continued use leads to physical dependence. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can trigger severe withdrawal, including seizures, agitation, insomnia, and anxiety rebound, sometimes lasting months.

Suicidality with antiseizure medications: All antiseizure medications, including clorazepate, have been associated with a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors. Monitor closely for mood or behavior changes.
Respiratory depression: Use with extreme caution in people with COPD, sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation, or other respiratory conditions.
Cognitive and motor impairment: Long-acting benzodiazepines increase risk of confusion, delirium, falls, and motor vehicle accidents, especially in older adults.

Paradoxical reactions: In some patients, especially children, older adults, and those with certain psychiatric disorders, clorazepate may cause agitation, aggression, or disinhibition rather than calming.
patient_counseling: Tell every clinician (especially if you see pain, surgery, or addiction specialists) that you are taking clorazepate.
Avoid drinking alcohol or using recreational drugs while on clorazepate—this greatly increases the chance of overdose and accidents.
Never take more than prescribed or share this medication with anyone else.
Do not stop clorazepate suddenly. Work with your prescriber on a slow taper plan.
Call for emergency help if you or someone else taking clorazepate is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or not making sense.
If you notice new or worsening depression, irritability, or thoughts of self-harm, contact your clinician immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Drowsiness, dizziness, cognitive slowing, and coordination problems are common. Long-term use increases risks of dependence, withdrawal, and falls.
plain_language_list: Feeling very sleepy or groggy during the day
Dizziness or feeling off-balance, especially when standing up
Slowed thinking, memory problems, or trouble focusing
Dry mouth, stomach upset, or constipation
Mood changes, including depression or irritability

common.patient_note: Most people feel sleepy, especially when starting or increasing the dose. This can be helpful in severe anxiety but can impair driving, school, or work performance.
You may feel wobbly or off-balance. This significantly increases fall risk, especially in older adults or those with other medical issues.

common.symptom: Cognitive Effects (Confusion, Slowed Thinking, Memory Problems)
common.patient_note: Clorazepate can make you feel mentally slower, forgetful, or foggy. Tasks that require quick thinking or fine coordination may be harder.
Some people notice feeling more down, irritable, or emotionally blunted. Report any significant mood changes to your clinician.
Dry mouth, mild stomach discomfort, or constipation can occur. Staying hydrated and using sugar-free gum may help.
Vision may feel slightly blurry, especially at higher doses. Avoid driving or operating machinery if this happens.

serious: Severe respiratory depression: slow or shallow breathing, bluish lips, difficulty staying awake—especially when combined with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives.
Severe hypotension or cardiovascular instability: lightheadedness, fainting, chest pain, or palpitations.
Suicidal thoughts or behaviors: new or worsening depression, self-harm thoughts, or unusual behavior changes.
Paradoxical agitation or aggression: marked restlessness, anger, or disinhibited behavior.
Prolonged or complicated withdrawal symptoms after dose reduction or discontinuation: severe anxiety, insomnia, tremor, hallucinations, or seizures.

sections.heading: Important Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Clorazepate’s main interaction risks involve breathing, sedation, and additive CNS effects.

items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
items.action: Avoid if possible. If co-prescribed, use the lowest effective doses, shortest duration, and close monitoring. Consider prescribing naloxone and educating family members.

items.with: Alcohol, cannabis, and other sedatives (sleep medicines, antihistamines, some antipsychotics, muscle relaxants)
items.risk: Additive CNS depression, confusion, falls, and overdose risk.
items.action: Strongly limit or avoid concurrent use. If combinations are unavoidable, doses of all sedating agents may need to be reduced.

items.risk: Extreme sedation, respiratory depression, increased risk of dependence and withdrawal complications.
items.action: Avoid combining routinely. If switching from another benzodiazepine, use a structured cross-taper plan.

items.with: CNS depressant antiseizure drugs (eg, phenobarbital) and other anti-epileptics
items.risk: Additive sedation and potential for complex interactions with seizure thresholds.
items.action: Neurology should guide combination use; monitor sedation, mood, and seizure control closely.

items.risk: May alter levels of active metabolites (nordiazepam, oxazepam), affecting both efficacy and toxicity.
items.action: Consider dose adjustments and monitor clinical response and side effects more closely when adding or removing such medications.

sections.heading: Stopping Clorazepate Safely
sections.text: Because clorazepate is long-acting and forms active metabolites, tapers must be slow and individualized.
key_points: Never stop clorazepate suddenly after extended use. Abrupt discontinuation can trigger life-threatening withdrawal, including seizures and severe agitation.

For low or moderate doses with no benzodiazepine use disorder: A common approach is to reduce the total daily dose by about 20–25% every week, adjusting based on symptoms and available tablet strengths.

For high doses, multi-year use, or suspected benzodiazepine use disorder: Tapers are slower—often a 25% reduction every 1–2 weeks, slowing further near the end. Total taper duration can be several months (sometimes up to 6 months or more).
Early reductions are often easier; later stages may require very small dose decreases and longer intervals between cuts.
Withdrawal symptoms can include rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, irritability, and in severe cases psychosis or seizures. Any severe or unusual symptoms warrant urgent medical review.
In complex cases, transitioning to another benzodiazepine with more predictable pharmacokinetics may be considered under specialist supervision.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Psychiatry-Focused)
sections.text: Doses below are typical ranges; individual plans must be tailored to age, comorbidities, other medications, and treatment goals.

adult.anxiety_initial: 7.5–15 mg/day, often as 7.5 mg at bedtime or 7.5 mg 2–3 times daily.
adult.anxiety_titration: Increase in small steps (eg, 7.5 mg/day) every 3–4 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.anxiety_typical: Around 30 mg/day in divided doses is common for anxiety; some patients may require higher doses, but risks increase significantly.
adult.anxiety_max: Up to 60 mg/day in divided doses, though many clinicians avoid the upper range due to sedation and dependence risk.
adult.seizures_adjunct_initial: Up to 7.5 mg three times daily.
adult.seizures_adjunct_titration: Increase in ≤7.5 mg increments at weekly intervals as needed.
adult.seizures_adjunct_max: Up to 90 mg/day in divided doses as an adjunct to other antiseizure medications.
adult.elderly: Start much lower (eg, 3.75–7.5 mg/day) and titrate very cautiously. Many guidelines recommend avoiding clorazepate in older adults when possible.
adult.hepatic: Use with caution; start low and titrate slowly.
adult.renal: Use with caution; clorazepate is largely eliminated renally as metabolites, so accumulation can occur.

pediatric.partial_seizures_under_9: 0.3–0.75 mg/kg/day in 1–3 divided doses (or 3.75 mg once to three times daily initially), titrated weekly; maximum 3 mg/kg/day or 60 mg/day, whichever is less.
pediatric.partial_seizures_9_to_12: Up to 7.5 mg twice daily initially; increase by 7.5 mg/day at weekly intervals to a maximum of 60 mg/day.
pediatric.partial_seizures_adolescents: Up to 7.5 mg three times daily initially; usual range 0.5–1 mg/kg/day; maximum 90 mg/day.
pediatric.note: Pediatric use is typically focused on seizure management and should be directed by a pediatric neurologist. Benzodiazepine use for anxiety in youth is generally limited and short-term due to dependence and cognitive risks.

sections.simple_explanation: For anxiety, doses typically start low and are increased slowly until symptoms improve or side effects become limiting. For seizures, higher doses are often needed and titration is more structured, under neurology guidance. In all cases, the goal is to use the smallest effective dose for the shortest possible time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: The long half-life and active metabolites of clorazepate raise special concerns in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, and medically complex patients.
sections.pregnancy: Clorazepate is converted to nordiazepam, which crosses the placenta. Benzodiazepine exposure in pregnancy has been associated with neonatal sedation and withdrawal, and potential (though not definitively established) teratogenic risks. Use is generally avoided unless potential benefits clearly outweigh risks and safer alternatives are unsuitable. For epilepsy, seizure control remains critical in pregnancy—any changes to antiseizure regimens should be made cautiously in coordination with neurology and obstetrics.
sections.lactation: Nordiazepam is present in breast milk and can accumulate in nursing infants, leading to sedation, poor feeding, and weight issues. The manufacturer generally advises against breastfeeding while taking clorazepate. Shorter-acting benzodiazepines or non-benzodiazepine options are typically preferred if medication is required during lactation.
sections.pediatrics: Use in children is largely confined to seizure management. For anxiety, benzodiazepines are reserved for brief, specific indications under specialist care. Children are at higher risk for paradoxical agitation, behavioral disinhibition, and cognitive effects.
sections.geriatrics: Clorazepate is on the Beers Criteria list of potentially inappropriate medications in older adults due to increased risk of cognitive problems, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents, and because older adults clear long-acting benzodiazepines more slowly. If used at all, start with very low doses and consider alternatives first.
sections.hepatic: Because active metabolites rely on hepatic metabolism, liver impairment can increase and prolong effects. Use with caution and consider lower doses or alternative agents.
sections.renal: Metabolites are excreted mainly via the kidneys; renal impairment can lead to accumulation and prolonged sedation. Use cautiously and monitor for toxicity.

sections.heading: What Clinicians Monitor
items: Level of sedation and cognition: Is the patient too sedated to function safely at work, school, or home?
Respiratory status: Especially in patients with lung disease, obesity, sleep apnea, or concurrent opioid use.
Cardiovascular status: Blood pressure and heart rate, particularly in frail or older adults.
Signs of misuse or loss of control: Early refills, dose escalation, using medication differently than prescribed, or requesting multiple prescribers.
Withdrawal symptoms: If doses are missed or reduced too quickly—anxiety, tremor, insomnia, agitation, or seizures.
Mood and suicidality: New or worsening depression or suicidal thoughts, particularly because clorazepate is also an antiseizure medication.
Laboratory tests with prolonged use: Blood counts, liver enzymes, and renal function.
Falls and injuries: Especially in older adults or those with other risk factors.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Clorazepate is available mainly as oral tablets or capsules.
items: US Tablets (clorazepate dipotassium): 3.75 mg, 7.5 mg, 15 mg (generic).
Former US brand Tranxene-T: 7.5 mg tablets (discontinued but often referenced in older records).
All forms are taken by mouth and may be given with food or water to reduce stomach upset.

sections.heading: How Clorazepate Works
sections.text: Clorazepate itself is a prodrug. In the stomach, it is rapidly converted into nordiazepam, an active benzodiazepine. Nordiazepam then binds to benzodiazepine sites on GABA-A receptors in the brain, enhancing the effect of GABA, the main calming (inhibitory) neurotransmitter. This increases chloride ion flow into neurons, hyperpolarizing them and making them less likely to fire. The result is reduced anxiety, sedation, muscle relaxation, and—at higher doses—antiseizure effects.

sections.heading: Place in Modern Psychiatric Practice
sections.text: Clorazepate is an older, long-acting benzodiazepine. In today’s practice, guidelines generally recommend SSRIs/SNRIs and psychotherapy as first-line treatments for anxiety disorders, with benzodiazepines used sparingly and short-term, if at all. When a benzodiazepine is needed, shorter-acting agents with more predictable profiles are often preferred. Clorazepate’s long half-life, accumulation of active metabolites, and high fall and cognitive risk—especially in older adults—mean it is rarely the first benzodiazepine chosen and is often avoided entirely in geriatric and high-risk populations. It remains relevant mainly as an adjunct in seizure management and in legacy cases where long-term users are being carefully maintained or gradually tapered.

seo.title: Clorazepate (Tranxene): Anxiety, Seizures, Dosing, Risks & Withdrawal
seo.description: Psychiatry-focused guide to clorazepate (Tranxene): how this long-acting benzodiazepine works for anxiety and focal seizures, dosing ranges, serious risks with opioids, dependence, withdrawal, and safer tapering strategies.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current benzodiazepine safety warnings, antiseizure medication guidance, and modern psychiatric recommendations on limited, cautious use of long-acting benzodiazepines.

faqs.a: Clorazepate is a long-acting benzodiazepine used to manage anxiety disorders and as add-on therapy for focal (partial) seizures. In psychiatry today, it is generally considered an alternative or last-line medication due to its long half-life, high dependence risk, and strong sedative and cognitive side effects.

Most people start to feel calmer and more sedated within 30–60 minutes after taking a dose. Because it turns into nordiazepam, which lasts a very long time in the body, its effects can carry over into the next day—especially if you take it regularly.

faqs.q: How long does clorazepate stay in your system?
faqs.a: Clorazepate is quickly converted to nordiazepam, which has a half-life of about 20–160 hours. That means it can take many days for the drug to fully leave your system after you stop taking it, and it can be detectable in the body for an extended period.

Yes. Like all benzodiazepines, clorazepate can lead to misuse, addiction, and physical dependence, even when taken exactly as prescribed. The risk is higher with larger doses, long-term use, a personal or family history of substance use disorder, or when combined with alcohol or other drugs.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop clorazepate suddenly?
faqs.a: Stopping clorazepate abruptly after regular use can cause severe withdrawal, including anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, agitation, and seizures. Withdrawal can sometimes be prolonged and difficult to separate from the return of your original symptoms. Never stop suddenly—work with your prescriber on a slow taper plan.

faqs.q: Can I take clorazepate with opioids?
faqs.a: Clorazepate and opioids both slow down brain activity and breathing. Taking them together greatly increases the risk of life-threatening respiratory depression, coma, and death. If there is no alternative and both are absolutely necessary, they must be used at the lowest possible doses with very close monitoring and overdose education (including naloxone for opioid overdose).

faqs.q: Is clorazepate safe for older adults?
faqs.a: In general, no. Long-acting benzodiazepines like clorazepate are considered potentially inappropriate for most people 65 and older because they increase the risk of confusion, falls, fractures, and car accidents. If an older adult is already on clorazepate, clinicians often discuss slow tapering and switching to safer alternatives.

faqs.q: Can I drive while taking clorazepate?
faqs.a: Clorazepate can make you drowsy, slow your reaction time, and affect judgment. Do not drive or operate machinery until you know exactly how it affects you, and be especially cautious when starting the medication or changing the dose. Many people find they are not safe to drive on daytime benzodiazepines.

faqs.q: Can I use clorazepate during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Clorazepate and its active metabolite cross the placenta and enter breast milk. Use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding is generally avoided unless there is a strong medical reason and safer options are not appropriate. If you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding, discuss risks and alternatives with your psychiatrist, neurologist, and obstetric provider before making changes.

faqs.q: Are there safer alternatives to clorazepate for anxiety?
faqs.a: Yes. For most people, first-line treatments for anxiety include psychotherapy (such as CBT) and antidepressants like SSRIs or SNRIs, which do not carry the same dependence and overdose risks as benzodiazepines. Non-benzodiazepine options such as buspirone or certain anticonvulsants may also be considered. Clorazepate is usually reserved for short-term or special circumstances when other treatments are ineffective or inappropriate.
